woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The film's feminist empowerment themes are visible from the first trailer and present from the opening scene. Lily's journey of self-discovery, the critique of male violence, and the 'break the cycle' messaging are never hidden or delayed. Conservative viewers know exactly what they are walking into. The marketing - despite being criticized for being too light-hearted - never disguises the film's ideological framework. What you see advertised is what you get. This is not a bait-and-switch.

director.name: Justin Baldoni
director.ideology: PROGRESSIVE LEAN. Baldoni is a self-described activist who gave a viral TED Talk titled 'Why I'm Done Trying to Be Man Enough' about redefining masculinity. He has spoken extensively about toxic masculinity, vulnerability, and feminist allyship. He is a practitioner of the Baha'i faith and positions himself as a progressive voice within faith communities. He describes himself as a registered Independent who does not publicly endorse candidates.
director.profile: Iranian-Italian-American actor and filmmaker. Baldoni rose to prominence playing Rafael Solano on Jane the Virgin (2014-2019). He founded Wayfarer Studios with a stated mission to create content that 'changes hearts and minds.' His directorial debut was Five Feet Apart (2019), a teen romance about cystic fibrosis. His second feature, Clouds (2020), was a true-story drama for Disney+. It Ends with Us is his third feature and biggest commercial success. Baldoni also hosts the podcast 'Man Enough,' which explores masculinity through a progressive lens. His approach to It Ends with Us was explicitly activist - he repeatedly stated in press interviews that the film needed to handle domestic violence responsibly and challenge how audiences think about abusers.

writer.name: Christy Hall
writer.profile: American playwright turned screenwriter. Hall began her career writing plays in New York City, supporting herself with bartending and dog walking. Her feature directorial debut was Daddio (2023), a two-hander starring Dakota Johnson and Sean Penn about a woman's confessional conversation with a taxi driver. Her It Ends with Us adaptation was her breakthrough studio project. Hall also served as a producer on the film. Her writing focuses on women's interior emotional lives, intimate conversations, and the complexity of female relationships with men. She has spoken about centering Lily's perspective and agency in the adaptation.

lead_producer.name: Alex Saks, Jamey Heath, Blake Lively, Christy Hall

composer.name: Rob Simonsen & Duncan Blickenstaff
composer.profile: Rob Simonsen is a versatile film composer known for The Way We Get By, The Spectacular Now, and Foxcatcher. Duncan Blickenstaff is a composer and music supervisor. Their score for It Ends with Us leans into romantic piano motifs and emotional string arrangements that complement the film's melodramatic tone without overpowering it.

top_performers.name: Justin Baldoni
top_performers.note: Baldoni is the film's standout performance and it is not even close. His Ryle is charming, vulnerable, and terrifying - often within the same scene. He plays the abuser not as a mustache-twirling villain but as a man who genuinely loves Lily and genuinely cannot control his rage. The complexity is essential to the film's message and Baldoni delivers it with precision. The breakfast scene where he burns his hand and reflexively slaps Lily is sickening precisely because Baldoni has made us like Ryle just minutes earlier.

top_performers.name: Isabela Ferrer
top_performers.note: As young Lily, Ferrer brings fragile warmth to the flashback sequences. Her chemistry with Alex Neustaedter's young Atlas provides the film's most emotionally honest scenes. The rooftop conversations feel unforced and genuine in a way that the adult timeline sometimes does not. Ferrer makes young Lily's hope feel real and her eventual heartbreak feel earned.

top_performers.name: Jenny Slate
top_performers.note: Slate brings natural comic warmth to Allysa, Ryle's sister. Her comedic timing provides relief from the film's heavier scenes without undercutting them. When Allysa confronts the truth about her brother's violence, Slate shifts gears convincingly from comedy to devastation. She insists that Lily never take Ryle back - a moment that lands because Slate has made us care about both the friendship and the family bond being torn apart.

bottom_performers.name: Blake Lively
bottom_performers.note: Lively is the film's weakest link in a role that demands enormous range. She is competent in the lighter romantic scenes but struggles to convey the deep trauma and psychological complexity that Lily's journey requires. Her line readings in the most devastating scenes - the staircase push, the attempted assault - feel surface-level rather than gutting. Multiple critics noted that Lively plays Lily as though she wandered in from a romantic comedy and never fully adjusts to the darkness. The character's internal turmoil - loving a man who hurts her, recognizing her mother's history repeating - needs an actress who can communicate agony through stillness. Lively communicates through aesthetics.

bottom_performers.name: Brandon Sklenar
bottom_performers.note: Sklenar's Atlas is underwritten and under-performed. He is meant to represent the road not taken - the good man who got away - but comes across as a generic attractive placeholder. His adult Atlas lacks the specific charm and vulnerability that Neustaedter brings to the younger version. The character functions as a plot device rather than a person, and Sklenar does not elevate the material beyond what is on the page.

fidelity_casting.summary: It Ends with Us is an adaptation of a contemporary novel with no prior screen versions. The casting is faithful to the source material's character descriptions. Lily Bloom is described as a young woman in her early twenties - Lively at 36 is notably older but the film adjusts the character's age accordingly. Ryle is described as tall, handsome, and charming - Baldoni fits. Atlas is described as dark-haired and athletic - Sklenar fits. The supporting cast aligns with the book's descriptions. No characters have been race-swapped or gender-swapped from the source material. The most significant adaptation choice is structural: the film intercuts young Lily's flashbacks with the adult timeline, giving the childhood abuse and first love story more weight than it carries in the novel's linear narrative. This is a creative choice, not an ideological one.

celebrity_mentions.name: Blake Lively
celebrity_mentions.context: Lively's press tour became the film's biggest controversy. She promoted her hair care line Blake Brown during interviews, encouraged audiences to 'grab your girlfriends' and wear florals to the theater, and treated a domestic violence drama like a lifestyle branding opportunity. She was widely criticized for tone-deaf marketing that trivialized the film's subject matter. In December 2024, she filed a sexual harassment complaint against Baldoni and Wayfarer Studios, alleging hostile workplace conduct and a retaliatory smear campaign. She also commissioned an alternative edit of the film, sidelining Baldoni in post-production. The behind-the-scenes drama overshadowed the film itself.

celebrity_mentions.name: Justin Baldoni
celebrity_mentions.context: Baldoni optioned the novel in 2019 and championed the project for years. His press tour focused heavily on domestic violence resources and survivor support - a stark contrast to Lively's approach. He was largely excluded from joint promotional events, fueling public speculation about on-set conflict. In January 2025, Baldoni counter-sued Lively, Ryan Reynolds, and their publicist for defamation and civil extortion. He also sued The New York Times for libel over their coverage of Lively's allegations. The legal battle remains unresolved.

celebrity_mentions.name: Ryan Reynolds
celebrity_mentions.context: Reynolds reportedly wrote 'a large chunk' of the rooftop dialogue scene between Lily and Ryle, allegedly without Baldoni's knowledge. His involvement in an uncredited capacity added to the perception that Lively was creatively hijacking the production. Reynolds is also named as a defendant in Baldoni's counter-lawsuit.

celebrity_mentions.name: Colleen Hoover
celebrity_mentions.context: Hoover's 2016 novel was a BookTok phenomenon that sold over 20 million copies. She publicly sided with Lively during the controversy and stepped back from social media amid separate criticism of her work's handling of domestic abuse themes. The New Statesman described her novels as 'profoundly sexually conservative' despite their feminist surface themes. She has declined to speak publicly about her political views.

content_warnings: Domestic violence depicted on screen - a husband slaps, pushes down stairs, and attempts to sexually assault his wife
Childhood domestic abuse depicted in flashbacks - a father physically abuses his wife while his daughter watches
Attempted marital rape scene - intense and disturbing, the wife escapes but the scene is prolonged
A teenage boy is severely beaten by an adult man
Emotional manipulation and gaslighting throughout - the abuser minimizes his violence and begs for forgiveness repeatedly
A character reveals he was suicidal as a teenager
A backstory reveals a child accidentally shot and killed his sibling, resulting in lifelong trauma
Moderate romantic and sexual content - kissing, implied sexual encounters, a morning-after scene
Brief alcohol consumption at social events
No strong profanity, no drug use, no nudity
family_discussion_topics: The film portrays how domestic violence can happen in seemingly loving relationships. Parents should discuss warning signs - the cycle of violence followed by apology and promises to change - with teenage viewers.
Lily recognizes that she is repeating her mother's pattern. How do generational cycles of abuse form, and what does it take to break them?

Ryle's childhood trauma - accidentally killing his brother - is offered as context for his violence but explicitly not as an excuse. The film distinguishes between understanding why someone is broken and accepting their behavior. This is worth discussing.

Lily chooses divorce to protect her daughter. The film frames this as an act of courage, not failure. Conservative families may want to discuss how the sanctity of marriage intersects with the safety of a spouse and child.
Atlas tells Lily she inspired him not to end his life. This provides a sensitive entry point for discussing mental health with older teenagers.
parental_guidance.recommendation: Not appropriate for children under 14. The domestic violence depictions are realistic and psychologically intense rather than graphic. The attempted rape scene, while not explicit, is deeply disturbing. The film's power comes from showing how charming and loving an abuser can be between episodes of violence - this complexity requires mature viewers who can process it critically. Parents of teenagers who have read the book should watch together and discuss the differences between romantic fantasy and real-world relationship dynamics.

summary.overall:
It Ends with Us arrives with more off-screen baggage than any film in recent memory. The Blake Lively vs. Justin Baldoni legal war, the tone-deaf press tour, the Ryan Reynolds ghost-writing controversy, the dueling edits - all of it threatens to overshadow what is, at its core, a competent domestic violence drama carried by one outstanding performance and one central question that conservative audiences should find surprisingly resonant: when do you break the cycle?

The plot is straightforward. Lily Bloom (Blake Lively) is a young woman who watched her father beat her mother throughout her childhood. She moves to Boston, opens a flower shop, and meets neurosurgeon Ryle Kincaid (Justin Baldoni), who is charming, intense, and emotionally volatile. They fall in love. He starts hitting her. Meanwhile, flashbacks reveal Lily's first love - Atlas Corrigan (Brandon Sklenar), a homeless teenager she sheltered as a girl, who her father nearly killed. Atlas resurfaces in Lily's adult life as a successful restaurant owner, complicating everything.

The film's greatest strength is its refusal to make Ryle a cartoon villain. Baldoni plays him as a man who is genuinely in love, genuinely remorseful after each violent episode, and genuinely unable to stop. This is what makes domestic violence so insidious in real life - the abuser is not always a monster. Sometimes he is a brilliant neurosurgeon who makes you laugh, who your friends adore, whose sister is your best friend. Baldoni understands this because he directed the film with an activist's intentionality, and his performance reflects it. The breakfast scene - Ryle burns his hand, reflexively slaps Lily, then collapses into horrified apology - is the film's most effective sequence because it captures the speed at which love turns to violence and back again.

The flashback structure works better than it should. Young Lily (Isabela Ferrer) and young Atlas (Alex Neustaedter) have genuine chemistry that the adult actors cannot match. Their rooftop conversations feel unscripted and real. When we learn that Atlas was suicidal the night Lily found him, and that she literally saved his life by being kind, the emotional weight lands. These scenes function as the film's moral compass - showing what healthy, tender first love looks like against the wreckage of what Lily's adult relationship becomes.

Blake Lively is the film's problem. She is not bad - she is insufficient. Lily Bloom requires an actress who can communicate the slow, devastating realization that the man she loves is going to kill her if she stays. Lively communicates the surface of this journey without ever reaching the depths. Her best moments are the lighter ones - the flower shop scenes, the early flirtation with Ryle. Her worst moments are the ones that matter most. When Ryle pushes her down the stairs and she lies at the bottom, Lively looks upset. She should look shattered. When Ryle attempts to rape her and she fights him off, Lively plays panic. She should play the death of everything she believed about her life. The gap between what the scene requires and what Lively delivers is the difference between a good movie and a great one.

Brandon Sklenar's adult Atlas is a void. The character is meant to represent the path Lily should have taken - the good man, the safe harbor. But Sklenar plays him as a handsome blank, a walking plot device who exists solely to give Lily somewhere to go when Ryle becomes dangerous. The young Atlas is vibrant and specific. The adult Atlas is a restaurant owner with good hair.

Jenny Slate, by contrast, is a revelation. Her Allysa provides comedy and warmth in the first two acts, then delivers the film's most devastating emotional moment when she confronts the truth about her brother. Slate tells Lily that Ryle accidentally killed their brother Emerson as a child, that the trauma manifests as uncontrollable rage, and that Lily must never take him back. It is the scene where the film earns its complexity - Allysa loves her brother and knows he is dangerous, and Slate plays both truths simultaneously.

Now for what our audience cares about. Is this film woke? The answer is more complicated than the discourse suggests.

The feminist empowerment framework is real and undeniable. The film is built on the premise that women must recognize patterns of male violence and choose themselves. Lily's journey from victim to survivor is framed as a feminist awakening. She names her daughter Emerson - the same name as the brother Ryle killed - as a symbolic act of reclaiming the cycle. The final line, 'It ends with us,' is a declaration of female agency. The film positions leaving an abuser as the ultimate act of empowerment.

But here is what the culture war discourse misses: this is also a profoundly traditional film.

Lily's decision to leave Ryle is not driven by ideology. It is driven by motherhood. She looks at her newborn daughter and realizes she will not let this child grow up watching what she watched. When she tells Ryle she wants a divorce, he resists - until she asks him how he would react if someone did to Emerson what he did to Lily. He agrees because even the abuser recognizes that protecting your child is non-negotiable. This is not a feminist argument. This is a parental one.

The film treats marriage seriously. Lily does not leave lightly. She tries to make it work. She accepts his apologies. She moves back in after the staircase incident. The divorce is presented as a last resort driven by the safety of a child, not as a casual lifestyle choice. Conservative viewers who value marriage will find that the film respects the institution even as it acknowledges that some marriages must end.

The generational abuse theme is classically conservative in its moral structure. Lily watched her mother endure decades of beatings. She is determined not to repeat that pattern. 'It ends with us' is not a progressive slogan - it is a declaration that moral courage means breaking cycles of sin, even when it costs you everything. This is Sunday morning sermon material dressed in a BookTok aesthetic.

Colleen Hoover's source material has been described by the New Statesman as 'profoundly sexually conservative' - men protect, women nurture, and every protagonist ends up pregnant. The film preserves this framework. Lily's pregnancy is the catalyst for her moral awakening. Atlas's love is protective and patient. Ryle's violence is treated as a moral failing rooted in childhood trauma, not as a systemic indictment of masculinity.

The off-screen controversy, ironically, may be the film's most ideologically charged element. Lively treating a domestic violence drama as a branding opportunity for her hair care line - telling audiences to 'grab your girlfriends and wear your florals' to a movie about a woman getting beaten by her husband - represents the worst of celebrity feminism. Baldoni, for all his progressive language about redefining masculinity, actually took the film's subject matter seriously on his press tour. The public turned on Lively not because she was woke but because she was shallow.

The box office tells a clear story: $351 million worldwide on a $25 million budget. This is a massive commercial success driven almost entirely by women aged 18-34 who read the book on BookTok. The film tapped a genuine cultural nerve about domestic violence, and audiences responded despite - or perhaps because of - the behind-the-scenes chaos.

RT Critics: 57% (Rotten). RT Audience: 88% (Hot). IMDB: 6.3. CinemaScore: A-. Metacritic: 52. The critic-audience gap is telling. Professional critics found the film tonally uneven and Lively miscast. Audiences - particularly women who connected with Hoover's novel - found it emotionally powerful. Both readings have merit.
summary.verdict_explanation: TRADITIONAL LEAN (+8 margin). This film scores traditional despite its feminist surface because the core values driving the narrative are deeply conservative. Lily leaves her husband not for self-actualization but to protect her child. The generational abuse cycle is treated as a moral imperative to break, not as systemic critique. Marriage is respected as an institution even as this specific marriage must end. The source material is sexually conservative - pregnancy as catalyst, men as protectors, traditional romance as the goal. The woke elements are real: feminist empowerment framing, a toxic masculinity subtext, and girl boss independence coding. But they are organically woven into a story about domestic violence, which inherently involves gendered power dynamics. The authenticity multiplier correctly reduces these scores. This is not ideological injection - it is the natural framework of a domestic violence story told from a woman's perspective.
summary.woke_trap_assessment: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The film's feminist themes are visible from frame one. The trailers show domestic violence. The marketing - despite Lively's tone-deaf approach - never disguises the subject matter. There is no bait-and-switch. What you see is what you get.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults should approach It Ends with Us with calibrated expectations. The feminist empowerment language is persistent but the underlying values are traditional: protect your children, break cycles of sin, take marriage seriously enough to end one that is destroying you. Baldoni's performance as Ryle is genuinely excellent and worth watching for the craft alone - he makes you understand how intelligent women stay with dangerous men. Lively is adequate but will not move you. The domestic violence sequences are realistic and disturbing rather than graphic. If you have personal experience with domestic violence - as a survivor, a child of survivors, or a professional who works with survivors - this film will hit differently than it hits casual viewers. That is its strength and its limitation: it is a film that works best for people who already understand what it is trying to say.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated PG-13 for domestic violence, sexual content, and thematic material. Recommended for ages 14 and up with parental accompaniment. The domestic violence is depicted realistically - a slap, a push down stairs, an attempted sexual assault. These scenes are not gratuitous but they are intense and psychologically disturbing. The film's power comes from showing a loving relationship that becomes dangerous, which can be confusing for younger viewers who may not understand the manipulation dynamics. The accidental sibling death backstory and a character's suicidal history are heavy themes. Moderate romantic content including kissing and implied sex. No nudity, no strong language, no drug use. For conservative families with teenage daughters, this is actually a valuable film to watch together - it illustrates warning signs of abusive relationships, the cycle of violence and apology, and the courage required to leave. Watch it with your kids and talk about it afterward.

tropeAudit.name: Feminist Empowerment Narrative
tropeAudit.analysis: Lily's arc is explicitly framed as a feminist journey from victim to empowered survivor. She recognizes the pattern of male violence in her life, chooses herself and her daughter over her marriage, and delivers the title line as a declaration of female agency. The empowerment framework is organic to a domestic violence story told from a woman's perspective - this is not ideological injection but the natural lens for this subject matter. Authenticity is high because telling this story without feminist framing would be dishonest to the material.

tropeAudit.name: Toxic Male / Patriarchal Violence
tropeAudit.analysis: The film's central conflict is male violence against women, depicted across two generations. Andrew beats Jenny. Ryle beats Lily. The pattern is presented as a feature of patriarchal family structures where men control through physical dominance. Ryle's violence is rooted in childhood trauma (accidentally killing his brother), which the film presents as context but explicitly not as excuse. Baldoni's direction ensures we understand Ryle as a specific broken man rather than a representative of all masculinity, but the generational framing carries implicit systemic critique. Authenticity is high because domestic violence is, statistically and historically, a gendered phenomenon. The film is depicting reality, not fabricating a narrative.

tropeAudit.name: Girl Boss Independence
tropeAudit.analysis: Lily opens her own flower shop, builds a successful business, and achieves financial independence before and during her relationship with Ryle. Her entrepreneurship functions as both character development and a symbol of self-sufficiency that makes her eventual departure from Ryle logistically possible. The film does not treat her business success as a substitute for relationships - she wants love, family, and partnership alongside professional fulfillment. This is closer to traditional self-reliance than progressive girl boss ideology, but the framing codes it as female empowerment. Authenticity is high because the business subplot is central to the source material.

tropeAudit.name: Celebrity Feminism as Brand Extension
tropeAudit.analysis: This scores as a meta-textual woke trope rather than a narrative one. Lively's press tour treated domestic violence as a lifestyle branding opportunity - promoting hair care products, encouraging floral-themed theater outfits, and avoiding substantive engagement with the film's themes. This represents the commodification of feminist messaging: domestic violence awareness becomes a marketing vehicle. The low authenticity reflects that this packaging was clearly manufactured rather than organic to the film itself. The film's text is more serious than its star's promotion of it.

tropeAudit.name: Breaking the Cycle of Abuse
tropeAudit.analysis: The entire film is structured around a single moral imperative: Lily must not repeat her mother's mistake. She watched her mother endure decades of abuse from her father. She recognizes the same pattern emerging in her own marriage. Her decision to leave is framed not as self-actualization but as moral courage - the hardest right thing she has ever done. 'It ends with us' is a declaration that generational sin must be confronted and stopped, regardless of the personal cost. This is deeply conservative moral theology: you are responsible for breaking the cycles you inherited.

tropeAudit.name: Maternal Protection
tropeAudit.analysis: Lily's pregnancy is the catalyst for her moral awakening. Before the baby, she can rationalize staying - he only did it once, he was triggered, he will get help. After the baby, the calculus changes absolutely. She looks at her newborn daughter and knows with certainty that she will not raise this child in a house where Daddy hits Mommy. The film treats motherhood as the force that gives Lily the strength to do what she could not do for herself alone. This is as traditional as storytelling gets: a mother protecting her child is the highest moral calling.

tropeAudit.name: Consequences of Moral Failure
tropeAudit.analysis: Ryle faces genuine consequences. He loses his wife, his daughter's full-time presence, and his self-image as a good man. The film does not give him a redemption arc or suggest that therapy will fix everything. His final scene - agreeing to the divorce after Lily asks how he would feel if someone hurt Emerson - is the moment where even the abuser acknowledges that his actions have destroyed something irreparable. Lily's father is given a blank eulogy at his funeral - Lily stands in silence because she cannot name five good things about him. Actions have permanent consequences. The dead do not get retroactive mercy.

tropeAudit.name: Sibling Loyalty and Family Bond
tropeAudit.analysis: Allysa's arc is built on the tension between loving her brother and protecting her friend. When she learns the truth about Ryle's violence toward Lily, she does not hesitate - she tells Lily to leave and never go back. But this decision costs her. The film shows that Allysa is torn, that choosing Lily means partially losing Ryle, and that this sacrifice is real. Family loyalty is treated as sacred but not unconditional - when a family member becomes dangerous, love requires hard choices. Jenny Slate plays this arc with understated devastation.

tropeAudit.name: Romantic Love as Redemptive Force
tropeAudit.analysis: Atlas's love for Lily spans decades. He was a suicidal homeless teenager when Lily found him, and her kindness literally saved his life. He named his restaurant after her. When she needs help, he is there without hesitation or agenda. The film presents their love as patient, enduring, and ultimately redemptive - the kind of love worth waiting for, contrasted against Ryle's passionate but destructive version. The final scene - Lily and Atlas meeting at the farmers' market, smiling - is a quiet promise that authentic love survives. This is traditional romantic idealism: the right person is worth the pain of getting there.

tropeAudit.name: Self-Worth and Walking Away
tropeAudit.analysis: Lily's journey is ultimately about recognizing her own worth. She internalized her mother's passivity as normal. She made excuses for Ryle the way her mother made excuses for her father. The moment she stops - the moment she says 'I deserve better than this and so does my daughter' - is the film's moral climax. The film treats self-worth not as narcissistic self-care but as the foundation of moral agency. You cannot protect others if you do not believe you are worth protecting yourself. This is a conservative message delivered through a feminist vehicle.
